title: Israeli president picks Gadi Eisenkot, Netanyahu rival, to try to form government
gist: After a deadlocked October 27 election, Israeli President Herzog tasked Gadi Eisenkot, Netanyahu's strongest rival, with forming a government; Netanyahu's bloc fell to 53 of 120 seats and Eisenkot's to 48, Arab parties won an unprecedented 19, and analysts see all three of Eisenkot's coalition paths as unlikely, raising the odds of prolonged deadlock or another election.

insights.claim: Likud won the most seats of any party with 27 in the 120-seat Knesset, but Netanyahu's religious-nationalist coalition won only 53 seats in total, short of the 61-seat majority.
insights.speaker: Al-Monitor
insights.so_what: Netanyahu has lost his governing majority — major regime shift risk for Israeli policy.

insights.claim: Eisenkot's Yashar party became the second-largest party with 21 seats, while his four-party centre-left to right-wing Jewish-led coalition won just 48 seats.
insights.speaker: Al-Monitor
insights.so_what: Neither bloc can govern alone; kingmakers are Arab and ultra-Orthodox parties.

insights.claim: Two parties representing Israel's Arab minority won an unprecedented 19 seats, and Arab leaders nominated Eisenkot first despite his refusal to join forces with them, giving him the most endorsements.

insights.so_what: Arab parties' record strength is a structural shift in Israeli coalition math.

insights.claim: President Isaac Herzog chose Gadi Eisenkot to try to form a government following a deadlocked election that left neither he nor Netanyahu with a clear path to power.
insights.speaker: Al-Monitor
insights.so_what: Start of a weeks-long coalition process; policy uncertainty elevated.

insights.claim: Eisenkot has 28 days to form a government with a possible 14-day extension; if he fails another candidate can try, then parliament can nominate someone, within a roughly 100-day process before a new election is held.
insights.speaker: Al-Monitor
insights.so_what: Sets a ~100-day window for political uncertainty; a repeat election is the fallback.
insights.quote: There is a deadline for the process of around 100 days.
insights.locator: Weeks of protracted negotiations are expected

insights.claim: Eisenkot's possible routes to power are a minority government relying on Arab party votes on key issues, a coalition with ultra-Orthodox parties he has shunned, or a unity government with Netanyahu — and analysts say all three are unlikely.
insights.speaker: Al-Monitor
insights.so_what: High probability of extended deadlock and possibly another election.
insights.quote: Analysts say that all three options are unlikely to take shape.
insights.locator: Weeks of protracted negotiations are expected

insights.claim: Eisenkot called for a 'national emergency government' after his nomination.
insights.speaker: Al-Monitor
insights.so_what: Signals a broad-unity framing to lure defectors.
insights.quote: Now is the time to form a national emergency government.

insights.claim: Eisenkot, 66, a former military chief and son of Moroccan immigrants, would be Israel's first prime minister from the Mizrahi community; he entered politics only in 2022.
insights.speaker: Al-Monitor
insights.so_what: Generational/identity shift in Israeli leadership if he succeeds.

insights.claim: Eisenkot briefly served in Netanyahu's wartime cabinet after the October 7, 2023 Hamas attack, then returned to opposition, rebuked Netanyahu's management of the Gaza campaign and swore never to serve with him.
